name: during (D io_uring wrapper)
baseline: C liburing echo server (MarkReedZ/mrloop) and C++ epoll echo server (methane/echoserver), both built with -O3; in the httpbench suite also the C liburing HTTP-reply server
workload: Single-threaded echo server, 50 clients, 512-byte messages, 10 s, best of 3, driven by haraldh/rust_echo_bench on loopback; second data set is a fixed-reply HTTP responder under wrk at 2 to 256 connections in tchaloupka/httpbench.
claimed_speedup: echo_server README: during 131090 req/s vs C liburing server 95894 req/s vs C++ epoll server 45063 req/s (1.37x and 2.91x, derived from page data). httpbench README (separate harness, D port of the C liburing server, RPS from the tables): during/raw vs C io_uring raw is 41404 vs 37872 (2 clients), 86500 vs 75711 (8), 150752 vs 155627 (64), 221916 vs 185000 (128), 253256 vs 246812 (256), 2012380 vs 1898736 (256 clients, pipeline depth 10), i.e. 0.97x to 1.20x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: during echo server: dub build -b release --compiler=ldc2, ldc2-1.18.0. Baselines: built with -O3 and no -g (compiler name and version not stated). httpbench D builds: ldc2 1.29.0 with --betterC --release -O3 --boundscheck=off --ffast-math --mcpu=native; C baseline gcc -Wall -O3 -D_GNU_SOURCE -luring (gcc version not stated, liburing cloned from axboe/liburing at build time).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X 8-Core, Fedora 31 Linux 5.3.12 (echo_server README); httpbench: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (8 cores, 16 threads) host, Fedora 36, kernel 5.17.9; server in a KVM VM with 2 pinned CPUs and load generator (wrk 4.1.0) in a KVM VM with 14 pinned CPUs, both Ubuntu 22.04 (bridged network)
tradeoffs: D library (druntime or betterC), Linux 5.7+ io_uring only; the echo example preallocates fixed io buffers registered with io_uring and can exceed the memlock limit; the library does not use liburing, so it reimplements the ring handling in D.
caveats: First-party numbers from the library author. The baselines are different programs, not a port: mrloop is an event-loop library and the C++ epoll echo server is a generic echo server, whereas the during example uses a fixed memory pool and buffer swapping, so the echo comparison is not same-algorithm. The echo README numbers come from 2019-era tools (ldc2-1.18.0, Linux 5.3.12, io_uring just introduced) and best-of-3 on loopback with one client machine; compiler versions of the baselines are missing. The httpbench rows are single 30 s runs per cell on a 2-vCPU server VM; the D port beats the C port in 5 of 6 cells (up to 1.20x) and loses by 3% at 64 clients, which is within plausible run-to-run noise for single runs, and the D build adds --mcpu=native while the C build does not. The httpbench README itself says the D variants exist to test performance issues of the during library, not to claim a win. The during README makes no performance claim and only points to the echo example. The echo-server category fits 'serving' loosely: it is a socket event loop, not an HTTP server.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch for a same-HTTP-server-in-several-languages comparison led to github.com/tchaloupka/httpbench, whose C-versus-D raw servers pointed to the during library and its echo_server README.
why_faster: io_uring with provided buffers and fixed pre-registered io buffers (README design notes); the source does not explain why it beats the C liburing server.

name: D (LDC, betterC) port of the C epoll raw HTTP responder (httpbench)
baseline: the C epoll raw HTTP responder in the same suite (c/epoll/http_epoll.c, gcc -O3), same fixed 'Hello, World!' reply, prefork over 2 CPUs
workload: Fixed-response HTTP/1.1 keep-alive responder (no parsing, no routing) under wrk for 30 s at 2, 8, 64, 128 and 256 connections, plus 256 connections with pipeline depth 10; level-triggered and edge-triggered variants, prefork over 2 pinned CPUs.
claimed_speedup: No claim in the README; the tables show parity. Level-triggered D vs C RPS: 43752 vs 39886 (2 clients), 93942 vs 88906 (8), 176532 vs 187141 (64), 232039 vs 226433 (128), 276433 vs 261440 (256), 2075254 vs 2132917 (pipelined); edge-triggered D vs C: 43096 vs 39911, 86692 vs 85850, 166672 vs 173116, 234975 vs 216984, 261737 vs 258486, 1938169 vs 2005563. Ratios 0.94x to 1.10x (derived from page data); D ahead in 8 of 10 non-pipelined cells (behind at 64 clients) and about 3% behind in both pipelined cells.
compiler_and_flags: D: ldc2 1.29.0, --betterC plus default --release -O3 --boundscheck=off --ffast-math --mcpu=native (_suite/runner.d); C: gcc -Wall -O3 -D_GNU_SOURCE (c/epoll/Makefile), gcc version not stated (Docker image debian:testing build-essential).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (8 cores, 16 threads) host, Fedora 36, kernel 5.17.9; server in a KVM VM with 2 pinned CPUs and load generator (wrk 4.1.0) in a KVM VM with 14 pinned CPUs, both Ubuntu 22.04 (bridged network)
tradeoffs: betterC @nogc D, i.e. D used as a C replacement without druntime, GC or exceptions; a micro benchmark that does not parse HTTP, so it says nothing about a real server.
caveats: This is a parity data point, not a win: counting the 10 non-pipelined cells, D is ahead in 8 and behind in 2 (64 clients, both variants) by at most 10%, and behind by about 3% (0.97x level, 0.97x edge) when pipelined; single 30 s runs with no variance reported, so the differences are probably noise. The D build uses --mcpu=native and --ffast-math while the C build uses plain -O3 without -march=native, so SIMD target is not matched (irrelevant for a syscall-bound loop). The C code is frevib's echo server slightly modified and the D file is a near line-by-line port using libc calls. The source states no mechanism and no claim (the suite's own C directory README says the D variants exist to test performance issues of the during library), which caps the tier at C. Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant. Last commit 2022-05-30.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'same HTTP server implemented in C++ Rust Go Zig io_uring epoll comparison benchmark github repo' surfaced tchaloupka/httpbench.

name: fasthttp in httpbench (Go vs nginx)
baseline: nginx (nginx-light package from the Debian testing Docker image; config c/nginx/nginx.conf: 'return 200' fixed reply, access log off, keepalive_requests 300000, reuseport; worker_processes 1 or auto via run.sh)
workload: Plaintext fixed-reply HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, wrk 30 s, server on 2 pinned vCPUs, 2 to 256 connections and 256 connections with pipeline depth 10.
claimed_speedup: Mixed. fasthttp vs nginx RPS: 36821 vs 36888 (2 clients, 1.00x), 74729 vs 80765 (8, 0.93x), 98288 vs 128320 (64, 0.77x), 104319 vs 128322 (128, 0.81x), 110780 vs 146610 (256, 0.76x), and with pipeline depth 10 at 256 clients 552677 vs 200126 (2.76x). Ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.18.x (README table says go1.18.1, Dockerfile installs 1.18.2), default go build flags; nginx is the distro build (version printed by the Dockerfile but not recorded in the README)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (8 cores, 16 threads) host, Fedora 36, kernel 5.17.9; server in a KVM VM with 2 pinned CPUs and load generator (wrk 4.1.0) in a KVM VM with 14 pinned CPUs, both Ubuntu 22.04 (bridged network)
tradeoffs: Not net/http compatible; the README itself says net/http is better for most cases.
caveats: Evidence for the known fasthttp entry (is_evidence_for_known), and it is counter-evidence for a 'faster than nginx' reading: fasthttp loses to nginx by 7% to 24% at 8 to 256 connections without pipelining and wins only when requests are pipelined, where nginx handles pipelined requests poorly. Single runs per cell, 2 server vCPUs, results from 2022 (Go 1.18, wrk 4.1.0). The suite's test code for fasthttp parses HTTP but has no router and a prebuilt reply, while nginx uses a 'return' directive with an extra X-Test header, so work per request is similar but not identical. Run by a third party (not the fasthttp author), code public: tier A.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'same HTTP server implemented in C++ Rust Go Zig io_uring epoll' surfaced tchaloupka/httpbench; rows read from its README results tables.

name: linkerd2-proxy (Rust) vs Envoy as service-mesh sidecars
baseline: Envoy (C++), as the Istio sidecar proxy
workload: Linkerd versus Istio service-mesh benchmark on the Kinvolk service-mesh-benchmark harness (wrk2 load against emojivoto instances, 500 to 5000 RPS steps, Equinix Metal cluster); per-proxy memory, CPU and added latency.
claimed_speedup: From search snippets only (pages not opened): at 4000 RPS Linkerd proxies held about 14-15 MB of memory against 135-175 MB for Envoy, and about 15 CPU-ms against 22-156 CPU-ms per instance; a later Buoyant run (Linkerd 2.10.2 vs Istio 1.10.0) reported Istio adding 36% more median latency and 438% more maximum latency at the highest load, with Envoy proxies using about 8x the memory and CPU of Linkerd's Rust proxies.
hardware: Equinix Metal (per harness README, machine type not stated on the opened page)
stars_or_usage: about 2.1k stars; data plane of the Linkerd service mesh
tradeoffs: Purpose-built for Linkerd (mTLS, retries, load balancing for sidecar use), not a general reverse proxy; far smaller feature surface than Envoy.
caveats: Snippet only: linkerd.io, buoyant.io and the CNCF mirror are unreachable here (DNS block), so none of the numbers were read on their page; the opened pages carry no results. The linkerd2-proxy README has no benchmark, and the harness repo kinvolk/service-mesh-benchmark (Apache-2.0, archived 2024-02-06, 142 stars, wrk2 at 120 s and 3000 RPS by default, 500-5000 RPS steps) lists no results. The comparison is Linkerd versus Istio, so the Envoy side reflects Istio's sidecar configuration and feature set, and the vendor (Buoyant) has a commercial stake; the authors themselves called it not an entirely fair comparison. The language is not isolated from the design difference. Tier C at best until a page with numbers is opened.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Linkerd2-proxy Rust vs Envoy C++ service mesh benchmark latency CPU memory Kinvolk' (snippets from Buoyant and Linkerd posts); repo and harness opened on github.com.
why_faster: Purpose-built minimal sidecar proxy in Rust versus the general-purpose Envoy (design scope, per the vendor); the language effect is not isolated.
